title: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
hook: two sisters bet on the color of a horse's tail, and one wins by sending her snake sons to cheat
carry: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame

segments.voice: Yesterday in the Adi Parva: Ruru's stick, and a harmless snake who taught him not to harm. Did one bad experience try to speak for a whole group? Day seven hundred.

What color is a white horse's tail? That's the bet between two sisters. They're both wives of the sage Kashyapa, Kadru and Vinata, and they've just seen a marvelous white horse, Uchchaihshravas, which rose from the churning of the ocean. Vinata says the horse is white all over. Kadru says no: its tail is black. They make it a wager, and the stakes are steep: the loser becomes the winner's slave. They agree to go and look. Before they do, Kadru calls her sons. Her sons are snakes. Today we reach the root of the snake sacrifice.
screen: `A WHITE HORSE FROM THE OCEAN.` → `A BET ON ITS TAIL.` → `THE LOSER BECOMES A SLAVE.`

segments.voice: Kadru tells her snake sons: go and hang on the horse's tail, like black hairs, so I win. Some of them refuse. And Kadru, furious, curses the ones who refuse: they will burn in the fire of a snake sacrifice held by a king named Janamejaya. That's the line the whole frame hangs on. The fire we met on the first day was spoken over these snakes long before Janamejaya was born. And the text adds a hard detail. Brahma, the creator, hears the curse and lets it stand, because the snakes, the text says, had become fierce and poisonous, a danger to other creatures. So a mother's curse becomes part of a larger order. Then the bet plays out. The tail looks black, Vinata loses, and she becomes her sister's slave. The Adi Parva doesn't pretend any of this is simple. Kadru wins by a trick. And look who the curse falls on: not the cheat, but the sons who said no to cheating. The text doesn't explain that away or soften it. It leaves the unfairness on the page, with the creator's assent beside it, and lets the listener feel how uneasy that is. In Sanskrit, Janamejaya's rite is called the sarpasatra, the snake sacrifice, and its fire will come long afterward, lit by a king who thinks only of his father. And one more thread starts here. Vinata has a son still to come out of his egg, a great bird. He'll be the one to set her free.
screen: `HANG ON THE TAIL LIKE BLACK HAIRS.` · `A CURSE ON THE SONS WHO REFUSED.` · `BRAHMA LETS IT STAND.` · `VINATA LOSES, AND SERVES.` · then, large: `SARPASATRA: THE SNAKE SACRIFICE.`

segments.voice: Settle in, and let a few breaths pass. Bring to mind a time someone asked you to help them win by bending something: cover for them, shade a number, take their side before you knew the facts. Maybe you said yes. Maybe you said no, and it cost you. Don't grade either. Just remember how the asking felt in the body: the chest, the jaw, the hands. Breathe in, and feel that pull. Breathe out, and notice the room where a no can live. The bell holds the time.
Adi Parva. The opening book, where a mother's curse on her snake sons sets the snake sacrifice in motion.

howItsDone: In some regions Hindu families honor snakes, nagas, at the festival of Nag Panchami. In the Adi Parva, Kadru's curse is the snakes' own family story: why the fire was coming for them.
